lead: A vehicle has more than one voltage domain. The 12 V bus runs lamps, ECUs and relays from the battery and alternator. The ignition secondary makes kilovolts for the spark plug. Advanced electric vehicles add a traction bus near 400 V. Fuses, relays, contactors and isolation checks keep these domains apart. This chapter maps the distribution path and its safety devices. It keeps the 12 V backbone separate from ignition kilovolts and EV traction volts.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for the 12 V battery, Chapter 1.4 for the regulated supply, and basic electrical safety.

sections.h3: The 12 V backbone and its protection

blocks.text: The battery positive terminal feeds a main fuse. This fuse protects the thick battery cable from a short circuit. After the main fuse, the cable reaches a fuse and relay box. Fuses protect each branch circuit; a fuse melts when current exceeds its rating. Relays are electrically controlled switches: a small current in the coil closes heavy contacts for a large load. The ignition switch or a push-button controls many relay coils. Electronic control units (ECUs) are electronic loads on protected branches; they need a stable supply. Wire gauge is chosen from load current and allowed voltage drop. Voltage drop is V = I × R, where V is volts, I is amperes and R is ohms. A long thin wire or a dirty ground adds R, so the load sees less than battery voltage. Chassis ground uses the steel body as the return path; bond straps connect panels and engine. Keep ground points clean and tight. The 12 V bus is a tree of protected branches, with the main fuse at the root.

sections.h3: Ignition secondary: a separate high-voltage circuit

blocks.text: Ignition secondary is a separate high-voltage circuit. The ignition coil has a primary winding and a secondary winding on one magnetic core. Current in the primary builds a magnetic field. When the ignition module interrupts that current, the field collapses and induces a high voltage in the secondary by mutual inductance. In older engines, a distributor routes the secondary pulse to each spark plug. In coil-on-plug (COP) systems, a small coil sits above each plug. Suppression leads are resistive spark-plug cables; they reduce radio-frequency interference and arc current. The secondary voltage rises until the gap ionises at breakdown, then falls to the low arc voltage that sustains the arc. Spark generation and timing belong to Unit 2. The secondary can shock; treat it as high voltage.

blocks.where: V<sub>s</sub> is secondary peak voltage in volts; V<sub>p</sub> is primary peak voltage in volts; N<sub>s</sub> is secondary turns; N<sub>p</sub> is primary turns.

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach the EV traction part. A traction battery works at about 400 V class, not 12 V. Two heavy contactors connect the battery to the inverter, which is a DC-to-AC converter for the motor. Contactors are relays built for high current and high voltage. The service disconnect is a manual switch or plug that separates the battery for maintenance. Orange cable marks the high-voltage path. An isolation monitor measures resistance between the high-voltage conductors and chassis; low isolation means a fault. The EV still has a 12 V bus, fed by a DC-DC converter, for lamps and ECUs. Do not mix this domain with ignition secondary kilovolts or the 12 V bus.

items: Check isolation before closing any contactor.
Close the pre-charge contactor through a resistor.
Close the main contactor; then open the pre-charge path.
Open contactors on fault or key-off.

examples.question: An ignition coil has a turns ratio of 100:1 (secondary turns to primary turns). The primary current is interrupted at a peak of 350 V. Find the ideal maximum secondary peak voltage. The spark plug gap breaks down at 8 kV. Find the reserve voltage (headroom) above breakdown.
steps: Primary peak voltage V<sub>p</sub> = 350 V; turns ratio N<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>p</sub> = 100.
Ideal maximum secondary peak V<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>p</sub> × (N<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>p</sub>) = 350 V × 100 = 35,000 V = 35 kV. This is the most the coil can produce.

The secondary voltage rises until the plug gap ionises at breakdown, V<sub>ion</sub> = 8 kV. It then falls to the arc voltage, a few hundred volts, which sustains the arc. The arc current comes from energy stored in the coil's magnetic field.
Reserve voltage (headroom) = V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>ion</sub> = 35 kV − 8 kV = 27 kV. This is spare capability to fire a wider, worn or fouled gap; it is not a voltage driving the arc.
examples.answer: The ideal maximum secondary voltage is 35 kV. The gap breaks down at about 8 kV, then the voltage falls to the arc voltage of a few hundred volts. The 27 kV difference is headroom that lets the coil fire a wider, worn or fouled gap; it does not appear across the arc.

traps: Domain mix-up: ignition secondary is kilovolts; EV traction is hundreds of volts; the 12 V bus is neither.
Primary versus secondary: the coil primary is a low-voltage winding; the secondary is the high-voltage winding.
Fuse job: a fuse limits current to protect wiring; it does not set or limit spark voltage.
Voltage drop: a high-resistance wire or ground drops volts only when current flows; an open circuit can show full voltage with no current.
EV pre-charge: the pre-charge resistor is not the main contactor; it limits capacitor inrush before the main contactor closes.

quiz.q: Which device protects the battery cable from a short circuit?
What colour commonly marks EV high-voltage cable?
Why is the ignition secondary high voltage when the coil primary is low voltage?
quiz.a: Mutual inductance and a high turns ratio step up the interrupted primary voltage; the secondary has many more turns.

quiz.q: Why use a relay instead of a switch for a large load?
quiz.a: The relay coil needs small control current; its contacts carry the large load current, keeping heavy wiring away from the dash switch.

quiz.q: A 12 V lamp draws 4 A. The feed wire and ground return total 0.25 Ω. Find the voltage drop and the lamp terminal voltage.
quiz.a: Taking the lamp current as about 4 A, V = 4 A × 0.25 Ω = 1 V, so lamp voltage ≈ 12 V − 1 V = 11 V. With the exact circuit the current falls slightly (about 3.7 A for a 3 Ω lamp), giving about 11.1 V.

quiz.q: An ignition coil has a turns ratio of 80:1 and a primary peak of 300 V. Find the ideal secondary peak in kV.
A technician measures 12.6 V at the battery and 10.9 V at the headlamp socket with the lamp on. Give the likely cause and explain why the lamp still lights.
quiz.a: High resistance in the feed or ground path. Current causes a 1.7 V drop, so the lamp gets less voltage but still lights, likely dim.

quiz.q: Why must pre-charge happen before the main EV contactor closes?
quiz.a: It limits inrush current into the inverter capacitors. Without it, the main contactor can weld or the fuse can open.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses high-voltage interlock loops, isolation monitoring and service disconnects; research is moving to 800 V class traction and faster charging. Search terms: pre-charge circuit, contactor welding, isolation fault, coil-on-plug suppression.
